summary: The Meliae (also called the Meliads; Ancient Greek Μελίαι) were the nymphs of the ash tree in Greek mythology, with whom they shared their name. According to Hesiod's Theogony, they were born from the drops of blood that fell upon Gaia (Earth) when Cronus castrated his father Uranus, making them siblings of the Giants and the Erinyes. In a tradition drawn from Hesiod's Works and Days, the ash trees—perhaps the Melian nymphs themselves—were regarded as the progenitors of the Bronze race of men. Although usually understood as ash-tree nymphs, the term is sometimes taken more broadly to mean tree-nymphs in general.
etymology: The name Meliai derives directly from the Greek word for ash trees, meliai, so that the nymphs are properly "ash-tree" nymphs. Some scholars read the term more loosely as denoting tree-nymphs in general, probably without distinction of any particular species.

sections.heading: Etymology
paragraphs: The name of the Meliae comes directly from the Greek word for ash trees, meliai, identifying them as "ash-tree" nymphs. The singular form is Melia, and the figures are also called the Meliads.

Although the connection to the ash is the usual interpretation, the term is sometimes understood more broadly as meaning tree-nymphs in general, probably without distinction of any particular kind of tree.

sections.heading: Birth and Family
paragraphs: According to Hesiod's Theogony, the Meliae were born from the drops of blood that fell upon Gaia (Earth) when Cronus castrated his father Uranus. The same shedding of blood produced the Giants and the Erinyes (Furies), making the Meliae siblings of those primordial offspring of Earth.
In Hesiod's reckoning the term Meliae probably embraced all tree-nymphs, situating them among the earliest generation of nature spirits to spring from the wounded earth.

sections.heading: Mythology and Cult
paragraphs: In Hesiod's Works and Days, the ash trees—perhaps meaning the Melian nymphs—are said to have been the progenitors of the Bronze race of men, the third and warlike generation of humanity in Hesiod's myth of the ages.
The Meliae also appear as caretakers of the infant Zeus. In one tradition they nursed the young god in the Dictaean mountains of Crete, feeding him on the milk of the goat Amalthea and on honey.

Individual nymphs bear the name Melia, among them a Theban nymph who became a consort of Apollo and the mother of Tenerus and Ismenus; in some accounts this Melia is instead reckoned an Oceanid, one of the daughters of Oceanus and Tethys.
